(3) MQTT-based metrics — tiny payloads published to a broker that feeds into Prometheus via Telegraf.

q: What are the differences between k3s, MicroK8s, and KubeEdge for edge Kubernetes?
a:
k3s: single binary (~70MB), full K8s API, SQLite/etcd backend, best for 1-10 node edge sites.
MicroK8s: snap-based, add-on system (gpu, istio, registry), best for Ubuntu-based edge.
KubeEdge: split architecture (CloudCore + EdgeCore), works with intermittent connectivity, edge nodes operate independently when disconnected, best for thousands of centrally managed devices.

q: What five mandatory security measures should be implemented on remote edge devices?
a:
(1) Encrypted storage with LUKS. (2) Signed OTA updates — verify with openssl before applying.
(3) Automatic certificate rotation with short-lived certs (hours, not years).
(4) Firewall with deny-all default and specific outbound allow rules only to control plane and MQTT broker.
(5) Read-only root filesystem using overlayfs for writable layers to prevent persistent malware.

q: How do you maintain remote access to edge devices over unreliable connections?
a:
Use autossh to maintain persistent reverse SSH tunnels with auto-reconnect: autossh -M 0 -f -N -R 2222:localhost:22 user@bastion with ServerAliveInterval/ServerAliveCountMax options.
Then SSH to the edge device via the bastion.
For interactive sessions, use mosh (mobile shell) which uses UDP, handles high latency, packet loss, and survives network changes and roaming.

q: Why must edge device designs assume power loss will happen, and what protections are needed?
a:
Edge devices lose power unexpectedly — no graceful shutdown. Use journaling filesystems (ext4, btrfs) to prevent corruption.
Make boot robust against unclean shutdowns. Never update a partition without A/B swap.
Additionally, design every protocol for intermittent connectivity — buffer data locally, retry with backoff.
The device should function (perhaps degraded) when completely offline.

q: What is the A/B partition scheme for OTA updates, and why is it essential for edge devices?
a:
The A/B partition scheme keeps two OS partitions: one active and one for updates. Updates are written to the inactive partition.
On reboot, the device tries the new partition.
If it fails to boot (3 consecutive failures), it automatically reverts to the previous partition.
This is essential because edge devices cannot be physically accessed for recovery if an update bricks them.

q: Why is standard Prometheus scraping unsuitable for edge devices on metered cellular connections, and what are two alternative strategies?
a:
Standard Prometheus pull-based scraping requires constant network availability and generates significant traffic that is expensive on metered cellular.
Alternatives: 1) Edge-local Prometheus with remote_write that batches and compresses metrics before pushing to a central server.

q: You manage 500 edge devices on cellular. An update bricked 3 devices in your canary group. What update safety rules should have prevented wider damage, and what is the correct phased rollout pattern?
a:
Safety rules: 1) Never update all devices at once — use canary deployment.
2) Every update must have automatic rollback (boot counter: if new version fails 3 times, revert; watchdog timer: if device does not phone home within N minutes, revert).
3) Never update the bootloader unless absolutely necessary.

q: What is the goal of a homelab in terms of fidelity?
a:
Pattern fidelity, not scale fidelity.
You don't need 1,500 servers to practice fleet management — you need 3-5 nodes with the same tooling patterns used in production.

q: What is the best bang-for-buck homelab hardware tier in 2025?
a:
The Mid Tier ($300-$800): 3x Intel N100 mini PCs with 16GB RAM, NVMe SSDs, a VLAN-aware managed switch, and a small UPS.
These are silent, low-power (~8W idle), and support Proxmox clustering with nested VMs.

q: What components does k3s ship with by default?
a: Traefik (ingress controller), CoreDNS (cluster DNS), Flannel (CNI), local-path provisioner (persistent volumes), and ServiceLB (LoadBalancer-type services using host ports).

q: What is the difference between VMs and LXC containers in Proxmox, and when should you use each?
a:
VMs are full virtual machines with their own kernel — use for Windows, appliances, or anything needing its own kernel.
LXC containers are lightweight Linux containers — use for services like PiHole and Gitea.
Proxmox also supports clustering (3+ nodes), live migration, templates, and multiple storage backends (local, NFS, Ceph, ZFS).

q: Why should you set up VLANs in a homelab, and what is a recommended VLAN layout?
a:
Network segmentation is a production skill worth practicing.
A recommended layout: VLAN 10 for management (Proxmox UI, switch), VLAN 20 for servers (VMs/containers), VLAN 30 for IoT/untrusted devices, VLAN 40 for Kubernetes pod network, VLAN 100 for WAN/Internet.
IoT devices should never share a network with Proxmox management.

q: What are the three tiers of essential self-hosted services for a homelab?
a:
Tier 1 (Infrastructure): PiHole (DNS), WireGuard (VPN), Traefik/nginx (reverse proxy + TLS).
Tier 2 (DevOps Practice): Gitea (Git), Prometheus + Grafana (monitoring), Loki (logs), ArgoCD (GitOps).
Tier 3 (Production Patterns): Nextcloud (storage), Keycloak (SSO/OIDC), MinIO (S3-compatible), Vault (secrets).

q: Why should you set up PiHole or local DNS on day one of your homelab?
a:
Accessing services by IP address is a recipe for confusion as your lab grows.
PiHole serves dual purposes: ad blocking and local DNS resolution for lab services using entries like proxmox.lab.home, grafana.lab.home, etc.
Point your DHCP server to use PiHole as primary DNS.

q: How do you create a cloud-init VM template in Proxmox for fast provisioning?
a:
Create a VM (qm create), import a cloud image disk (qm importdisk), configure the SCSI controller and boot disk (qm set --scsihw virtio-scsi-pci), add cloud-init drive (qm set --ide2 local-zfs:cloudinit), set serial console, configure IP (qm set --ipconfig0 ip=dhcp), then convert to template (qm template).
Clone from template with qm clone for each new VM.

q: What are the key components of a WireGuard VPN setup for accessing your homelab remotely?
a:
Generate server and client key pairs (wg genkey/wg pubkey), create server config (/etc/wireguard/wg0.conf) with PrivateKey, Address (e.g., 10.200.0.1/24), ListenPort (51820), PostUp/PostDown iptables rules for NAT masquerade, and Peer section with client's PublicKey and AllowedIPs.
Enable with systemctl, and port-forward 51820/UDP on your router to the WireGuard host.

q: What are the two most costly pitfalls when buying enterprise salvage hardware for a homelab?
a:
(1) Not checking power costs — a $150 Dell R730 can add $20-50/month to your power bill at 120-400W draw.
(2) Over-engineering on day one — you don't need Ceph, 10GbE, and a three-node HA Proxmox cluster to start.
Begin with one node and one k3s install. Complexity is the enemy of learning.

q: What is Proxmox VE and what does it replace in a homelab environment?
a:
Proxmox VE is a free, open-source hypervisor built on KVM/QEMU with a web UI. It replaces VMware vSphere for homelab virtualization.
It supports VMs, LXC containers, ZFS storage, clustering with HA, and live migration.

q: Why should you set up VLAN segmentation in a homelab even though it is 'just a lab'?
a:
Network segmentation is a core production skill that you should practice in a homelab.
IoT devices should not be on the same network as your Proxmox management interface.
VLANs prevent untrusted devices from reaching management planes, and practicing VLAN configuration (management, servers, IoT/untrusted, Kubernetes) builds muscle memory for real datacenter and cloud network design.

q: Describe the process to create a cloud-init VM template in Proxmox and use it to rapidly provision a 3-node k3s cluster.
a:
1) Create a VM shell: qm create 9000 --name ubuntu-cloud --memory 2048 --cores 2 --net0 virtio,bridge=vmbr0.
2) Import a cloud image as disk: qm importdisk 9000 ubuntu-cloud.img local-zfs.
3) Attach the disk and cloud-init drive: qm set 9000 --scsi0 local-zfs:vm-9000-disk-0 --ide2 local-zfs:cloudinit.
4) Convert to template: qm template 9000.

q: What is a Distinguished Name (DN) in LDAP, and what is an example?
a: A DN is the full path to an entry in the LDAP directory tree, read from the entry up to the root.

q: What are the two most common LDAP operations, and what does each do?
a:
BIND authenticates a client to the directory (verifies credentials).
SEARCH queries entries based on filters and scope (the most common operation). Other operations include ADD, MODIFY, DELETE, and COMPARE.

q: What does /etc/nsswitch.conf control, and what does "passwd: files sss" mean?
a:
NSS (Name Service Switch) controls the order in which the system looks up users, groups, and hosts.
"passwd: files sss" means look up users first in /etc/passwd (local files), then ask SSSD (which queries LDAP/AD).
The order determines fallback behavior.

q: What are the four PAM control flags, and why does their order matter?
a:
required (must pass, continues checking), requisite (must pass, stops immediately on failure), sufficient (if passes, skip remaining modules), optional (only matters if it is the only module).
Order matters because a misplaced "sufficient" can bypass all subsequent security checks.

q: What is SSSD, and what key problem does its caching feature solve?
a:
SSSD (System Security Services Daemon) connects Linux to LDAP/AD/FreeIPA for authentication and identity.
Its caching feature allows users to log in even when the LDAP server is unreachable — if the cache is warm with previously authenticated credentials, offline login succeeds.

q: How does LDAP filter syntax work, and how do you combine conditions with AND, OR, and NOT?
a:
LDAP filters use prefix notation with parentheses. Simple: (uid=alice). AND: (&(objectClass=posixAccount)(uidNumber>=1000)).
OR: (|(uid=alice)(uid=bob)). NOT: (!(loginShell=/bin/false)). Filters can be nested and combined for complex queries.

q: How does Kerberos provide single sign-on without sending passwords to services?
a:
The user authenticates once to the KDC (Key Distribution Center) and receives a TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket).
When accessing a service, the TGT is presented to the KDC to get a Service Ticket. The Service Ticket is presented to the service for access.
The user's password is never sent to the service.

q: Describe the full Linux authentication chain from user password entry to LDAP verification.
a:
User types password, which goes to PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules, configured in /etc/pam.d/).
PAM consults NSS (/etc/nsswitch.conf) for name resolution. NSS routes to SSSD (configured in /etc/sssd/sssd.conf, must be mode 0600).
SSSD queries the backend LDAP/AD/FreeIPA server. Each layer can fail independently, and knowing the chain is key to debugging login failures.

q: What does FreeIPA bundle together, and how does it compare to Active Directory?
a:
FreeIPA bundles LDAP (389 Directory Server), Kerberos, DNS, and a web UI into a single identity management platform.
It is the open-source answer to Active Directory, providing centralized authentication, authorization, host enrollment, sudo rule management, and SSH key distribution — all managed through a single CLI (ipa commands) or web interface.

q: How do you join a Linux machine directly to Active Directory using realmd, and what does the process configure?
a:
Run "realm discover ad.example.com" then "realm join ad.example.com -U admin".
This auto-configures SSSD for AD identity and authentication, Kerberos (/etc/krb5.conf), PAM, and NSS.
Verify with "realm list" and test with "id aduser@ad.example.com".
Configure "use_fully_qualified_names = false" in sssd.conf if you want short usernames.

q: What is a Distinguished Name (DN) in LDAP, and what are its components?
a: A DN is the full path to an entry in the LDAP directory tree, read from most specific to least specific.

q: Describe the Linux authentication chain from user login to LDAP, naming each component.
a: User types password -> PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules, configured in /etc/pam.d/) handles the authentication flow -> NSS (Name Service Switch, /etc/nsswitch.conf) maps identities (uid to username) -> SSSD (System Security Services Daemon) acts as the cache and backend connector -> LDAP/AD/FreeIPA backend validates credentials and provides identity data.

q: What do the PAM control flags 'required', 'requisite', 'sufficient', and 'optional' mean, and why does their order matter?
a:
required: must pass, failure is fatal but continues checking remaining modules.
requisite: must pass, failure stops immediately (no more modules checked).
sufficient: if it passes, skip remaining modules in this stack (success short-circuits).
optional: result only matters if it is the only module.

q: What is the first rule of the archaeological approach when inheriting a legacy system?
a:
Observe what exists first — don't change anything yet.
The previous team was not stupid; they were working with different constraints, solving different problems, under different time pressures, using the tools available at the time.

q: When Git says max_connections=100, the server says 500, and docs say 200, which is the real value?
a:
The server is real. Always. Git is what someone intended. The server is what's actually running.
Common causes of drift include manual hotfixes during incidents, config management running a different branch, and environment variable overrides.

q: Why are cron jobs described as "the dark matter of infrastructure"?
a:
Cron jobs are the tribal knowledge of a system — nobody documents them, nobody remembers adding them, and they run silently until they break.
They hold critical processes together and should be inventoried on day one when inheriting a system.

q: What commands should you run in the "First Day Survey" to understand an inherited system's purpose and network connections?
a:
For purpose: systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running.
For network listeners: ss -tlnp (TCP) and ss -ulnp (UDP). For active connections: ss -tnp to see what's talking to what.
Also check installed packages (rpm -qa or dpkg -l), cron jobs, and recently modified files in /etc.

q: What is the Config Reading Protocol for understanding configs you didn't write?
a:
Four steps: (1) Find the REAL config the process actually reads (check process cmdline, /proc/PID/cmdline).
(2) Identify what was customized vs. default (rpm -V or dpkg -V).
(3) Read for intent — comments are gold, look for TODO/HACK/FIXME and date-stamped comments.
(4) Map config interdependencies — includes, environment variables, templates vs. rendered configs.

q: Name four methods for tracing system dependencies when there is no documentation.
a:
(1) Network connections: ss -tnp shows TCP connections with process names.
(2) DNS lookups: tcpdump port 53 reveals what hostnames the system resolves.
(3) Filesystem reads: lsof -p PID shows open files, sockets, and libraries.
(4) Environment variables: cat /proc/PID/environ reveals database URLs, API endpoints, and integration points.

q: What are three signs that critical knowledge is trapped as tribal knowledge rather than documented?
a:
(1) A README says "ask Dave about the deployment process" but Dave left 2 years ago.
(2) A script references a path in a specific user's home directory as the canonical source.
(3) "We always restart it on the first Monday of the month" but nobody knows why.

q: How can you use systemd unit files to discover service dependencies and configuration sources?
a:
Run systemctl cat  to see the full unit file. After=, Requires=, and Wants= directives reveal ordered dependencies.
ExecStartPre= reveals setup steps that must run before the service.
Environment= and EnvironmentFile= reveal configuration sources.
You can also run systemd-analyze dot to generate a full dependency graph.

q: How do you use strace to find which config files a process actually reads at startup?
a:
Run strace -f -e openat  to trace all file open calls.
Filter out ENOENT (file not found) to see only files that were successfully opened.
For a running process: strace -f -e openat -p PID.
For nginx specifically: strace -f -e openat nginx -t 2>&1 | grep -v ENOENT.
This reveals the real config files versus what you assume they are.

q: Why should you "disable before deleting" when decommissioning legacy components, and what is the recommended waiting period?
a:
If you don't understand what something does, you can't know it's unused.
Disabling (rather than deleting) lets you observe whether anything breaks.
Wait at least a month after disabling before deleting.
Additionally, never change things before understanding them — observe for at least two weeks before making non-emergency changes to inherited systems.

q: When you inherit a system on your first day, what is the very first survey you should run before changing anything?
a:
Run: hostname && uname -a && cat /etc/os-release (identity), uptime (stability), systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running (purpose), ss -tlnp (network listeners), ss -tnp to map connections, crontab listings for all users, du -sh /* for disk usage, and awk -F: '$3 >= 1000' /etc/passwd for human users.
Observe before touching anything.

q: The config in git says maxconnections=100 but the running server has maxconnections=500. Which is the real config and how do you find what the process is actually using?
a:
The server is always the real config — git shows intent, not reality.
Find what the process actually uses by: 1) Check the process command line for config file paths: cat /proc//cmdline | tr '\0' ' '.
2) Use lsof -p  to see which config files are open.

q: You discover a cron job running a binary with no source code in the repo, as user 'jsmith' who left 2 years ago. How do you investigate what it does and whether it is safe to disable?
a:
1) Read the cron entry for schedule, command, and output destination.
2) Examine the binary: file , strings  to find clues.
3) Use strace or lsof to trace its system calls and network connections when it runs.
4) Check git log --all --author=jsmith for context.
5) Check if anything depends on its output (files it writes, services it signals).

q: What are the six key GPU metrics that ops engineers need to monitor?
a:
GPU utilization (%), GPU memory used (GB), GPU temperature (C), GPU power draw (W), PCIe throughput (GB/s), and NVLink throughput (GB/s).
Use nvidia-smi for snapshots and DCGM exporter with Prometheus for continuous monitoring.

q: What are the four layers of the CUDA stack from top to bottom, and why is version compatibility critical?
a:
Application (PyTorch/TensorFlow) -> CUDA Toolkit (nvcc, cuBLAS, cuDNN) -> CUDA Driver (nvidia.ko kernel module) -> GPU Hardware.
Compatibility is strict: toolkit version must match the application build, driver must be >= toolkit version, driver must support the GPU generation, and kernel version must be compatible with the driver.

q: How does GPU scheduling work in Kubernetes by default?
a:
Kubernetes doesn't natively understand GPUs — you need the NVIDIA device plugin (a DaemonSet).
GPU scheduling is all-or-nothing: if a pod requests 1 GPU, it gets exclusive access to that entire GPU.
No sharing, no overcommit. Verify GPUs with kubectl describe node | grep nvidia.com/gpu.

q: What is vLLM and how do you configure its Kubernetes deployment for production?
a:
vLLM is an LLM inference server.
Key deployment considerations: set gpu-memory-utilization (e.g., 0.90), mount a PVC for model cache (avoid re-downloading 140GB models on every restart), set initialDelaySeconds on readiness probes to 120+ seconds (models take minutes to load), mount /dev/shm as emptyDir with medium: Memory for PyTorch DataLoader.

q: What are the five common causes of GPU memory (VRAM) OOM errors and their fixes?
a:
(1) Batch size too large — reduce batchsize.
(2) Model doesn't fit in GPU memory — use model parallelism, quantization, or bigger GPU.
(3) Memory fragmentation in PyTorch — set PYTORCHCUDAALLOCCONF=expandable_segments:True.
(4) Memory leak in training loop — ensure tensors are detached/deleted.
(5) Multiple users sharing GPU via time-slicing — use MIG for memory isolation.

q: What are the three categories of ML storage needs and appropriate solutions for each?
a:
(1) Model weights (read-heavy, large files): NFS/NAS, S3 with local cache, or ReadWriteMany PVCs.
(2) Training data (read-heavy, massive): S3/GCS with streaming, Lustre/GPFS for HPC, or NFS with SSD cache.
(3) Checkpoints (write-heavy during training): local NVMe for speed, PVC for persistence, or S3 with periodic sync for durability.

q: Why is mounting /dev/shm critical for PyTorch training jobs in Kubernetes, and what happens if you forget?
a:
PyTorch DataLoader uses shared memory for multiprocess data loading. Default /dev/shm in Kubernetes is only 64MB.
A training job with 8 data workers will crash because it exceeds this limit.
Fix: mount an emptyDir with medium: Memory at /dev/shm with an appropriate sizeLimit (e.g., 16Gi).

q: Why should GPU nodes be tainted in Kubernetes, and what happens without taints?
a:
Without taints, Kubernetes will schedule CPU-only pods on expensive GPU nodes, consuming CPU and memory that GPU workloads need for data loading.
A GPU node with 4x A100s and 64 CPU cores might only run 4 pods (one per GPU), and the CPU/RAM exists to feed the GPUs.
Taint GPU nodes and tolerate only GPU workloads to prevent resource waste on $10K-$40K/card hardware.

q: What are the six critical alerts to configure for a GPU cluster and their severity levels?
a:
GPU memory > 90% VRAM (Warning), GPU temperature > 83C sustained (Warning — thermal throttling reduces performance 20-40%), GPU utilization < 10% for 30 min (Info — wasting money), XID errors detected (Critical — hardware errors), CUDA OOM pod restart (High), GPU not detected / nvidia-smi fails (Critical).
Use DCGM exporter Prometheus metrics for alerting.

q: Why is mounting /dev/shm as an emptyDir with medium: Memory critical for PyTorch training jobs in Kubernetes?
a:
PyTorch DataLoader uses shared memory (/dev/shm) for multiprocess data loading.
The default /dev/shm in Kubernetes is only 64MB.
A training job with multiple data workers will crash when it exceeds this limit.
Mounting an emptyDir with medium: Memory provides adequate shared memory backed by RAM.

q: What is the difference between GPU time-slicing and MIG (Multi-Instance GPU), and when would you use each?
a:
Time-slicing shares a GPU by rapidly switching between workloads but provides no memory isolation — all workloads share GPU memory, creating OOM risk.
MIG (available on A100/H100) partitions the GPU into hardware-isolated instances with dedicated memory.
Use time-slicing for development environments where cost matters more than isolation.

q: A GPU training job shows low GPU utilization (15%) despite requesting a full A100. What are three likely causes and how do you diagnose each?
a:
1) Data loading bottleneck — the CPU/disk can't feed data fast enough.
Diagnose with nvidia-smi showing GPU idle between bursts, and check CPU utilization and disk I/O.
Fix with more DataLoader workers or faster storage. 2) Small batch size — GPU finishes quickly and waits.
Diagnose by correlating batch size with utilization.

q: What are the three Kubernetes multi-tenancy models and their isolation levels?
a:
Namespace per tenant (isolation: 2/5, lowest cost, simplest), Virtual Cluster per tenant using tools like vCluster (isolation: 4/5, moderate cost, tenants get their own API server), and Dedicated Cluster per tenant (isolation: 5/5, highest cost, maximum isolation).
Namespace per tenant is the right starting point for most teams.

q: Why are resource quotas not optional in a multi-tenant Kubernetes cluster?
a:
Without quotas, one namespace can consume every CPU core and byte of memory in the cluster.
A single tenant's runaway deployment can starve all other tenants.
Once a ResourceQuota exists in a namespace, every pod must declare resource requests and limits or be rejected, forcing tenants to think about their resource needs.

q: What is the first network policy you should create in every tenant namespace?
a:
A default-deny-all policy with an empty podSelector and both Ingress and Egress policyTypes.
This ensures no pods can communicate with anything by default.
Then add explicit allow rules for intra-namespace traffic, DNS egress (port 53 UDP/TCP), and ingress from the ingress controller namespace.

q: What is the difference between ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges, and how do they work together?
a:
ResourceQuotas cap the total resources for an entire namespace (e.g., total 40Gi memory).
LimitRanges constrain individual containers and pods (e.g., max 8Gi per container, default 512Mi).
LimitRanges also inject default resource specs into pods that omit them, acting as a safety net so even forgetful tenants get sensible defaults instead of unbounded allocation.

q: What should tenant RBAC roles include and exclude in a namespace-per-tenant model?
a:
Include: get/list/watch/create/update/patch/delete on pods, deployments, services, configmaps, jobs, cronjobs.
Allow reading secrets but not creating/deleting. Allow pods/log and pods/exec.
Exclude: ClusterRole bindings, access to nodes/namespaces/persistentvolumes (cluster-scoped), escalate/bind verbs on roles (privilege escalation), and access to secrets in kube-system.

q: Why are priority classes important in a multi-tenant cluster and what is a recommended hierarchy?
a:
Without priority classes, pod eviction under resource pressure is arbitrary — your monitoring stack could be evicted alongside batch jobs.
Recommended hierarchy: system-critical (1000000) for cluster infrastructure, tenant-production (100000) for production workloads, tenant-development (10000, globalDefault) for dev/staging, tenant-burst (1000, preemptionPolicy: Never) for bes...

q: What is the critical prerequisite for network policies to actually work in a Kubernetes cluster?
a:
Network policies require a CNI that supports them, such as Calico, Cilium, or Weave.
If you use a CNI that does not enforce network policies (e.g., default kubenet), the NetworkPolicy objects exist in the API but have zero effect — traffic flows unrestricted between all pods despite the policies being defined.

q: What resources should be created as a unit when onboarding a new tenant, and why should this be automated?
a: Create as a unit: Namespace, ResourceQuota (compute and object limits), LimitRange (per-container defaults and caps), NetworkPolicy (default-deny plus explicit allows), Role (tenant-developer), RoleBinding (team to role), ServiceAccount (for CI/CD), and PriorityClass reference.

q: How does each isolation mechanism reduce the blast radius of a tenant mistake or compromise?
a:
Without quotas: one runaway tenant consumes all cluster compute. With quotas: constrained to allocation.
Without default-deny network policy: tenant can reach all pods in the cluster.
With default-deny: isolated to own namespace.

q: When should you upgrade from namespace-per-tenant to virtual clusters, and what does vCluster provide?
a: Upgrade when tenants need to install their own CRDs, need independent cluster-admin access, or when namespace-level isolation is insufficient (cluster-scoped resources are shared, compromised API server affects everyone).

q: Why must you create a default-deny NetworkPolicy before any allow rules in a multi-tenant cluster?
a:
By default, all pods can talk to all pods in Kubernetes.
In a multi-tenant cluster, this means tenant A's web server can reach tenant B's database.
A default-deny NetworkPolicy (empty podSelector, both Ingress and Egress policy types) blocks all traffic in the namespace, then you add specific allow rules on top.

q: What happens when a ResourceQuota exists in a namespace but a pod does not declare resource requests and limits?
a:
The pod is rejected by the API server.
Once a ResourceQuota exists in a namespace, every pod in that namespace must declare resource requests and limits.
This forces tenants to think about their resource needs.
To prevent this from breaking existing workloads, combine ResourceQuota with a LimitRange that provides default requests and limits for pods that omit them.

q: What are the three multi-tenancy models in Kubernetes, and when would you choose each?
a: Namespace per tenant (most common, low cost, moderate isolation — good starting point for most teams), virtual cluster per tenant using tools like vCluster (stronger isolation, tenants can install CRDs and have independent cluster-admin, higher complexity), and dedicated cluster per tenant (maximum isolation, no noisy-neighbor risk, but expensive and requires fleet management).

q: What are the five most common cause categories for infrastructure incidents, ranked by frequency?
a: (1) Recent change ~40%, (2) Resource exhaustion (disk, memory, CPU, connections) ~25%, (3) Dependency failure (upstream service, DNS, database) ~15%, (4) Time-based trigger (cron, cert expiry, log rotation) ~10%, (5) Traffic/load spike ~10%.

q: What is the most common cause when df shows 100% disk usage but du totals to much less?
a:
Deleted files still held open by a process. Unix doesn't free disk space until ALL file descriptors are closed.
Check with lsof +D /var/log | grep deleted, then restart the process holding the file descriptor.

q: An API has 2-second response time but CPU is at 10%, memory and disk are fine. What are the top three causes to investigate?
a:
(1) DNS resolution delays — check with time nslookup; if >100ms, add DNS caching.
(2) Connection pool exhaustion — application waiting for DB/Redis/HTTP connections.
(3) Upstream service is slow — your service is fast but waits on a dependency.
Also check TCP retransmissions (netstat -s | grep retransmit) and GC pauses.

q: A service is running (systemctl shows UP) but connections are refused. What are four possible causes?
a:
(1) Service listening on wrong interface (127.0.0.1 vs 0.0.0.0). (2) Firewall or security group blocking the port.
(3) TCP listen backlog is full under heavy load — increase net.core.somaxconn.
(4) File descriptor limit reached — the process can't open new sockets (check with cat /proc/PID/limits).

q: A server rebooted unexpectedly with no maintenance scheduled. What are the top four causes to investigate?
a:
(1) OOM killer invoked — check dmesg | grep "out of memory".
(2) Kernel panic — check journalctl -k -b -1 (previous boot). (3) Hardware watchdog timeout — dmesg | grep watchdog.
(4) Unattended OS updates with auto-reboot — check /var/log/unattended-upgrades/ or dnf history.
Also check UPS logs and cloud console event logs.

q: An application crashes every few hours with no error in app logs. What is the most common cause and how do you confirm it?
a:
OOM killer is the most common cause for silent process kills.
Confirm with dmesg | grep "Killed process" which shows the PID and memory usage at kill time.
Other causes: segfault (dmesg | grep segfault), resource limits hit (check /proc/PID/limits), systemd killing it (TimeoutStopSec/WatchdogSec), or another process sending a kill signal.

q: Explain the Differential Diagnosis Model for infrastructure debugging.
a: Like doctors, generate a list of possible causes ranked by probability, then systematically rule them out: (1) Observe symptoms, (2) Generate hypotheses, (3) Rank by probability, (4) Test the most likely hypothesis first (cheapest/fastest check), (5) If confirmed, remediate, (6) If not, eliminate and move to next, (7) If all eliminated, you're missing information — widen your view.

q: Name four investigation anti-patterns and their better approaches.
a:
(1) Anchoring: first theory becomes the only theory — write down 3 hypotheses before testing any.
(2) Confirmation bias: only seeking supporting evidence — actively try to disprove your theory.
(3) Tunnel vision: deep-diving one component — set 15-minute timeboxes.
(4) Heroics: one person debugging solo for hours — escalate at 15 minutes if no progress.

q: Disk I/O is slow but iostat shows under 50% utilization. What are four non-obvious causes?
a:
(1) I/O scheduler contention — multiple processes competing; use iotop to check per-process I/O.
(2) Filesystem journaling overhead — EXT4 with data=journal doubles write amplification.
(3) RAID rebuild in progress — cat /proc/mdstat to check.
(4) Thin-provisioned storage doing copy-on-write (LVM thin pools, ZFS, cloud EBS) — first write to a block is slower.

q: What single question resolves approximately 40% of production incidents within minutes?
a:
'Was anything deployed or changed in the last 4 hours?' Recent changes (deploys, config changes, infrastructure changes) are the number one cause of incidents at roughly 40% frequency.
If the answer is yes, there is a strong correlation — rollback first, investigate second.

q: df shows 100% disk usage but du -sh /* totals to only 60%. What are the most likely causes of the missing 40%?
a:
1) Deleted files still held open by a running process (most common) — check with lsof +D /var/log | grep deleted, fix by restarting the process.
2) Filesystem reserved blocks — ext4 reserves 5% for root by default, check with tune2fs -l.
3) A mount point covering a directory that has data underneath it — umount and check.
4) Large filesystem journal consuming space that du does not report.

q: API response time is 2 seconds but server CPU is at 10%, memory is fine, and disk is fine. Walk through the differential diagnosis.
a:
1) DNS resolution delays (extremely common) — test with 'time nslookup api.dependency.com', fix with local DNS cache.
2) Connection pool exhaustion — application waiting for database/Redis/HTTP connections, check pool metrics and ss -tnp ESTABLISHED count.
3) Upstream service is slow — your service is fast but blocks on a dependency, add timeouts and circuit breakers.

q: How does component thinking differ from systems thinking when diagnosing issues?
a:
Component thinking: "The database is slow" and "The API has high latency" — two separate problems.
Systems thinking: "The API retries on database timeouts, increasing database load, making it slower, causing more retries" — one feedback loop, one problem, fix the loop.

q: What is the difference between tight and loose coupling in infrastructure?
a:
Tight coupling: Service A directly calls Service B synchronously — A breaks when B breaks.
Loose coupling: Service A puts a message on a queue, Service B reads when ready — A survives B's failure.
The queue absorbs the shock.

q: Why can adding retries to fix a 10% error rate actually cause a total outage?
a:
If Service B is failing because it's overloaded, adding 3 retries to Service A increases load on B by up to 3x.
B's failure rate goes from 10% to 40%, then with retries the effective load becomes 4x, and B crashes completely.
The fix was correct in component thinking but catastrophic in systems thinking.
Use a retry budget instead: only retry if total retry rate is below 10% of requests.

q: What is emergent behavior and how does the "thundering herd" illustrate it?
a:
Emergent behavior is system-level behavior no individual component was designed to produce.
Thundering herd: each server individually does "when cache is empty, fetch from database" — correct for one server.
But 100 servers simultaneously discover the cache is empty, fire 100 identical queries, and collapse the database.

q: Describe the typical cascade that takes a system from a single database lock to total user-facing failure.
a:
(1) Database runs a long query with table lock. (2) API connections queue. (3) Connection pool exhausts.
(4) API returns 503s. (5) Load balancer marks API unhealthy. (6) Traffic shifts to remaining instances.
(7) They get 2x traffic and also exhaust. (8) All API instances down. (9) Users refresh, adding more traffic.
This can take under 60 seconds.

q: How do circuit breakers prevent cascading failures, and what are their three states?
a:
Circuit breakers sit between client and service.
Three states: CLOSED (normal, requests pass through), OPEN (errors exceeded threshold, requests fail immediately without calling the backend — prevents pile-up), HALF-OPEN (after cooldown, lets one test request through; if it succeeds, closes the circuit; if it fails, stays open).

q: Why do systems become nonlinear near capacity, and what is the critical insight about utilization?
a:
Queue theory shows that latency is not linear with load. Going from 70% to 80% utilization might add 10ms.
From 80% to 90% adds 100ms. From 90% to 95% adds 500ms.
Most production systems live at 70-80% capacity, where small load increases cause disproportionate latency spikes.
This is why capacity planning must leave headroom.

q: What is "fix-induced failure" and what six questions should you ask before implementing a fix?
a: Fix-induced failure is when each fix solves the local problem but creates a new one elsewhere (e.g., increase memory limit -> fewer pods per node -> can't scale -> add nodes -> more DNS queries -> CoreDNS overload).

q: What is a positive (reinforcing) feedback loop in infrastructure? Give an example.
a: A positive feedback loop amplifies change rather than stabilizing the system.

q: Explain Little's Law (L = lambda * W) and why a 'small' latency increase can cause a total outage.
a:
L (concurrent requests) = lambda (arrival rate) * W (average latency).
If your API handles 100 rps at 200ms, L = 20 concurrent requests.
If latency increases to 2 seconds (database hiccup), L jumps to 200.
Your connection pool of 50 is exhausted, requests queue, latency increases further, L grows more — a positive feedback loop.

q: Why can adding retries to a failing service make the failure worse? What is the systems-aware alternative?
a:
If Service B is failing at 10% because it is overloaded, adding 3 retries from Service A increases load on B by up to 3x.
B's failure rate rises from 10% to 40% or more, and with retries the effective load is 4x original — B crashes entirely.
The fix looks correct in component thinking but is catastrophic in systems thinking.

q: What VS Code extension provides Terraform syntax highlighting, autocomplete, and format-on-save?
a: The HashiCorp Terraform extension. It also provides go-to-definition for module references.

q: How do you split the integrated terminal in VS Code, and why is this useful for DevOps work?
a:
Use Ctrl+Shift+5 to split terminals.
This lets you run a watch command (e.g., kubectl logs -f) in one pane while editing in another, keeping monitoring and development side by side.

q: What VS Code setting trims trailing whitespace automatically, and in which file is it configured?
a:
files.trimTrailingWhitespace: true, configured in settings.json (user settings).
This helps maintain clean files across all DevOps file types.

q: What does the Remote-SSH extension allow you to do, and how does it work?
a:
Remote-SSH lets you connect to remote servers and edit files as if they were local.
You connect via Ctrl+Shift+P, "Remote-SSH: Connect to Host," and enter user@hostname.
VS Code then opens folders, runs terminal commands, and enables debugging — all on the remote machine using your ~/.ssh/config.

q: What problem do Dev Containers solve, and where is the configuration defined?
a:
Dev Containers guarantee every contributor has identical tools, versions, and extensions by defining the development environment as code.
Configuration lives in .devcontainer/devcontainer.json and can specify a base image, features (Docker, kubectl, Terraform), extensions, and post-create commands.

q: How do you automate common commands like linting and testing in VS Code?
a:
By defining tasks in .vscode/tasks.json. Each task specifies a label, type (shell), command, and group.
Run tasks via Ctrl+Shift+P, "Tasks: Run Task." You can set a default test task so it runs with a keyboard shortcut.

q: How does VS Code validate Kubernetes manifests and GitHub Actions workflows against their schemas?
a:
The Red Hat YAML extension validates files against JSON schemas.
Configure it in settings.json with "yaml.schemas" mapping schema URLs to file globs — e.g., "kubernetes" for k8s/*/.yaml and the GitHub workflow JSON schema for .github/workflows/*.yml.

q: What is a multi-root workspace, and when would a DevOps engineer use one?
a:
A multi-root workspace lets you open multiple separate directories (app, infrastructure, k8s-config repos) in a single VS Code window, defined in a .code-workspace file.
DevOps engineers use it when working across application code, Terraform modules, and Kubernetes manifests simultaneously, avoiding constant window switching.

q: How do you configure VS Code to debug a FastAPI application with breakpoints?
a:
Create a .vscode/launch.json configuration with type "debugpy", request "launch", module "uvicorn", and args pointing to the app module (e.g., "app.api.main:app", "--reload", "--port", "8000").
Set breakpoints by clicking the gutter, then press F5 to start debugging with full variable inspection.

q: How do you create environment-specific terminal profiles in VS Code, and why is this useful?
a:
Define profiles in settings.json under "terminal.integrated.profiles.linux" with a path, args that set environment variables (e.g., KUBECONFIG for staging vs production), and visual cues like custom icons and colors (red for production).
This prevents accidentally running commands against the wrong cluster.

q: What VS Code feature lets you edit files on a remote server as if they were local, and how do you connect?
a:
The Remote-SSH extension.
Connect via Ctrl+Shift+P -> 'Remote-SSH: Connect to Host', enter user@hostname (it uses your ~/.ssh/config).
Once connected, you can open folders, use the terminal, and debug — all running on the remote machine.

q: How do Dev Containers solve the 'works on my machine' problem for a DevOps team?
a: Dev Containers define the development environment as code in a .devcontainer/devcontainer.json file that specifies the base image, installed tools (docker, kubectl, helm, terraform), VS Code extensions, and post-create setup commands.

q: How would you configure VS Code terminal profiles to visually distinguish staging from production Kubernetes contexts and prevent accidental production commands?
a:
Create named terminal profiles in settings.json with different KUBECONFIG paths and visual indicators.
Set the staging profile with 'path: bash, args: [-c, export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/staging; exec bash]' and a server icon.

q: What are the three phases of the FinOps framework?
a: Inform (visibility into who spends what and why), Optimize (right-size, use commitments, eliminate waste), and Operate (continuous governance, budgets, alerts).

q: What are spot/preemptible instances and how much can they save?
a:
Spot instances cost 60-90% less than on-demand pricing but can be reclaimed by the cloud provider with 2-minute notice.
They are safe for stateless web apps, batch jobs, dev/staging environments, and CI/CD runners.

q: Describe the right-sizing process using VPA (Vertical Pod Autoscaler).
a:
1. Deploy VPA in "Off" (recommendation-only) mode. 2. Collect 7 days of usage data. 3.
Set requests to VPA's "target" recommendation. 4.
Set limits to 2-3x the request (or remove CPU limits for bursty workloads). 5. Monitor for OOMKills or throttling. 6.
Repeat quarterly.

q: What workloads are safe and unsafe for spot instances?
a:
Safe: stateless web apps with multiple replicas, retryable batch jobs, dev/staging environments, CI/CD runners.
Unsafe: single-replica databases, stateful workloads without graceful shutdown, long-running jobs that cannot checkpoint.

q: How does cross-AZ traffic drive cloud costs and how can you reduce it?
a:
In AWS, cross-AZ traffic costs $0.01/GB each way.
Reduce by enabling topology-aware routing (service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto) to prefer same-zone backends, using VPC endpoints for AWS services, and pulling container images from ECR in the same region.

q: How do you find and eliminate wasted storage in Kubernetes?
a:
Find unbound PVCs with kubectl get pvc -A | grep -v Bound.
Find PVCs not mounted by any pod by comparing PVC names to pod volume claims.
Use tiered storage: SSD for databases, HDD for logs and archives, object storage (S3/GCS) for long-term backups.

q: How does Karpenter differ from Cluster Autoscaler and what makes it more cost-effective?
a:
Karpenter provisions individual nodes based on pod requirements rather than scaling pre-defined node groups.
It can mix spot and on-demand, select from multiple instance types, consolidate underutilized nodes (consolidationPolicy: WhenUnderutilized), and auto-expire nodes for freshness.
This leads to better bin-packing and lower waste.

q: How do Pod Disruption Budgets protect applications on spot instances?
a:
A PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) sets minAvailable or maxUnavailable constraints.
When spot nodes are reclaimed, Kubernetes respects PDBs during eviction, ensuring at least the specified number of pods remain running.
This prevents too many replicas from being evicted simultaneously during spot reclamation events.

q: Name five cost visibility tools and their primary use cases.
a:
Kubecost (open source, per-namespace/pod cost allocation), OpenCost (CNCF project, standardized cost monitoring), CloudHealth (SaaS, multi-cloud enterprise), AWS Cost Explorer (native AWS analysis), GCP Billing (native GCP analysis).
Use Kubecost/OpenCost for Kubernetes-specific cost attribution and cloud-native tools for provider-level analysis.

q: In Kubernetes, what is the single biggest cost optimization opportunity, and why?
a:
The request/limit gap. You pay for requested resources, not actual usage.
If a container requests 500m CPU but only uses 100m, you are paying for 400m of idle capacity.
Right-sizing requests to match actual usage (using VPA recommendations) is the highest-impact cost optimization because it directly reduces the compute you are billed for across every pod.

q: What workloads are safe to run on spot/preemptible instances, and what workloads are not?
a:
Safe for spot: stateless web apps behind Deployments with multiple replicas, retryable batch jobs, dev/staging environments, and CI/CD runners.
Not safe: single-replica databases, stateful workloads without graceful shutdown, and long-running jobs that cannot checkpoint.
Spot instances cost 60-90% less but can be reclaimed with 2-minute notice.

q: What is Cilium and how does it differ from traditional CNI plugins?
a:
Cilium is a Kubernetes CNI plugin that uses eBPF instead of iptables for networking, security, and observability.
Traditional CNIs (Calico iptables mode, Flannel) use iptables/IPVS rules that scale poorly.
Cilium programs eBPF bytecode directly in the kernel, providing better performance and visibility at scale.

q: How do Cilium network policies differ from standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy?
a:
CiliumNetworkPolicy extends standard NetworkPolicy with L7 (HTTP, gRPC, Kafka) filtering, DNS-aware rules (allow traffic only to specific FQDNs), identity-based policies (instead of IP-based), and the ability to inspect and filter by HTTP path, method, and headers.
Standard NetworkPolicy only operates at L3/L4.

q: What is Hubble and what does it provide?
a:
Hubble is Cilium's built-in observability platform.
It provides network flow visibility (source, destination, protocol, verdict), service dependency maps, DNS query monitoring, HTTP request/response metrics, and real-time flow filtering.
Access via hubble CLI, Hubble UI (web dashboard), or Prometheus metrics export.

q: How does Cilium's eBPF datapath handle a packet?
a:
When a packet arrives, Cilium's eBPF program at the tc (traffic control) hook: 1) Looks up the source identity from the identity map.
2) Checks policy map for allowed identities. 3) Performs L3/L4 filtering.
4) Optionally inspects L7 via a userspace proxy (Envoy). 5) Forwards or drops.
All L3/L4 decisions happen in kernel space — no context switches.

q: What is a Cilium identity and how is it assigned?
a:
Cilium assigns numeric identities to endpoints based on their Kubernetes labels.
All pods with the same security-relevant labels share the same identity.
Network policies reference these identities instead of IP addresses, so policies survive pod restarts and IP changes.
Identity allocation is managed by the Cilium operator via a KVStore or CRDs.

q: How does Cilium replace kube-proxy?
a:
Cilium can run in kube-proxy replacement mode, handling Service load balancing entirely in eBPF.
Benefits: no iptables rules for Services (better performance at scale), Maglev consistent hashing for backends, socket-level load balancing (skipping NAT for local traffic), and DSR (Direct Server Return) mode for reduced latency.

q: What is Cilium Cluster Mesh and when would you use it?
a:
Cluster Mesh connects multiple Kubernetes clusters so pods can communicate across clusters using pod IPs.
Use cases: multi-cluster service discovery, cross-cluster load balancing, shared network policies, disaster recovery.
It works by synchronizing identities and service endpoints across clusters via etcd or CRDs.

q: How do you troubleshoot Cilium connectivity issues?
a:
1) cilium status — check agent health. 2) cilium endpoint list — verify endpoints are in "ready" state.
3) cilium policy get — check if policies are loaded. 4) hubble observe — watch live traffic flows and check for drops.
5) cilium monitor — low-level packet tracing. 6) Check cilium-agent logs for errors.

q: How does Cilium provide transparent encryption?
a:
Cilium supports WireGuard and IPsec for transparent pod-to-pod encryption without application changes.
WireGuard mode is simpler (one key pair per node), lower overhead, and recommended.
IPsec mode supports more compliance frameworks.
Both encrypt traffic between nodes while keeping intra-node traffic unencrypted (already isolated by cgroup).

q: What are the prerequisites for running Cilium?
a:
Linux kernel 4.19+ (5.10+ recommended for full features).
If replacing kube-proxy, start the cluster without it (--skip-kube-proxy in kubeadm).
Cilium can run alongside other CNIs in chaining mode but is best as the primary CNI.
Requires a KVStore (external etcd or CRD-based, which is default since Cilium 1.13).

q: What is Nodepool and how is it related to Zuul?
a:
Nodepool is a system for managing test node resources. It supports launching single-use test nodes from cloud providers as well as managing access to pre-defined pre-existing nodes."

"Zuul uses a separate component called Nodepool to provide the resources to run jobs.

q: What is a Pipeline in Zuul?
a:
A pipeline in Zuul is a workflow. This workflow can be executed based on different events - when a change is submitted to a project, when it's merged, etc. 
The pipeline itself can be applied on one or more different projects (= repositories in hosted or private source control)

q: Describe shortly what is Zuul
a:
From [Zuul’s docs](https://zuul-ci.org/docs/zuul/about.html): "Zuul is a Project Gating System. That’s like a CI or CD system, but the focus is on testing the future state of code repositories...

Zuul itself is a service which listens to events from various code review systems, executes jobs based on those events, and reports the results back to the code review system.

q: What is Zuul’s speculative merge (gating) model and how does it differ from traditional CI?
a:
In traditional CI, each change is tested independently against the current state of the repository.
Zuul’s speculative merge model instead tests each change as if all changes ahead of it in the gate queue have already merged.
This means Zuul predicts the future state of the repo and tests against that, catching integration conflicts before they land.

q: How does Zuul handle cross-project dependency testing?
a:
Zuul can natively test changes that span multiple projects (repositories) together.
When a change in project A declares a dependency on an unmerged change in project B (via a Depends-On header in the commit message), Zuul will check out and test both changes simultaneously.

q: What are the main Zuul configuration files and what does each one define?
a:
Zuul uses several YAML configuration files: .zuul.yaml (or zuul.yaml / zuul.d/ directory) — lives in each project repo and defines the jobs, project-pipeline bindings, and project templates for that repo.
main.yaml — the tenant configuration file on the Zuul server that defines tenants, their source connections, and which projects are included.

q: How does Zuul’s secrets management work, and why is it more secure than typical CI secret injection?
a:
Zuul encrypts secrets using per-project RSA keypairs.
Each project has a unique public key, and secrets are encrypted with that key and stored directly in the project’s .zuul.yaml file.
Only the Zuul executor with the corresponding private key can decrypt them at runtime.

q: What is the difference between a trusted and untrusted project in Zuul?
a:
Trusted (config) projects contain Zuul’s pipeline definitions, base jobs, and tenant configuration.
Changes to trusted projects are tested but only take effect after they merge.
Untrusted projects are application repos that consume pipelines and jobs defined by trusted projects.

q: What happens in Zuul’s gate pipeline when a change in the middle of the queue fails?
a:
When a change fails in the middle of the gate queue, Zuul dequeues that change and all changes behind it.
It then re-enqueues the changes that were behind the failed change, but now they are tested against the predicted state of the repo without the failed change.
For example, if changes A, B, C are queued: B is tested as if A merged, C is tested as if A+B merged.

q: What are Zuul’s Ansible-based jobs and how do they differ from shell-script-based CI jobs?
a:
Zuul jobs are defined as Ansible playbooks rather than shell scripts.
Each job specifies a playbook to run, a nodeset (target nodes), and optional parent jobs for inheritance.
Pre-run and post-run playbooks handle setup and teardown.
Benefits over shell-based CI: Ansible provides idempotent task execution, built-in error handling, structured output, and multi-node orchestration.

q: What is the 'impact formula' for writing strong resume bullet points as an ops engineer?
a:
[Action verb] + [what you built/changed] + [quantified result].
The result should include measurable metrics: time saved, scale (number of servers/services), reliability improvement (uptime %, MTTR reduction), cost savings, or risk reduction (incidents prevented, compliance achieved).

q: What is 'title arbitrage' in the ops job market, and how should you account for it when job hunting?
a:
Title arbitrage refers to the fact that identical work carries different titles at different companies — a 'Senior SysAdmin' at one company may do the same work as a 'DevOps Engineer' at another but at 60% of the salary.
When job hunting, search across all equivalent titles (SysAdmin, DevOps Engineer, SRE, Platform Engineer, Infrastructure Engineer, Cloud Engineer) to find the best opportunities.

q: What is the impact formula for ops resume bullets and what six types of quantification can be used?
a:
Formula: [Action verb] + [what you built or changed] + [quantified result].
Six quantification types: (1) time saved (hours/week, minutes per deploy), (2) scale (servers, services, users affected), (3) reliability (uptime %, MTTR reduction), (4) cost (dollars saved, resources reduced), (5) risk (incidents prevented, compliance achieved), (6) speed (deployment frequency, lead time improvement).

q: What is title arbitrage in ops job hunting, and why does searching only one title leave money on the table?
a:
Title arbitrage: the same skill set is labeled differently across companies — 'Senior SysAdmin,' 'DevOps Engineer,' 'Infrastructure Engineer,' 'Platform Engineer,' 'SRE' often describe the same work but at different salary bands.
Searching only one title means missing roles at higher comp.

q: What differentiates a Staff Engineer from a Senior Engineer in ops contexts, and why do most senior engineers stall at this transition?
a:
Senior engineers solve hard technical problems assigned to them.
Staff engineers identify which problems are worth solving across teams and set technical direction for the organization.
The differentiator is not deeper technical skill — it is organizational scope.

q: How do you open the Command Palette in VS Code?
a: Ctrl+Shift+P (or F1). This is the single most important shortcut -- it gives you searchable access to every command and setting in VS Code.

q: How do you quickly open a file by name in VS Code?
a:
Ctrl+P. Start typing the filename and it fuzzy-matches across the whole project.
Add : after the name to jump to a specific line number (e.g. main.py:42).

q: How do you open VS Code Settings?
a:
Ctrl+, opens the Settings UI.
To edit the raw JSON: Ctrl+Shift+P then type "Preferences: Open Settings (JSON)".
User settings apply everywhere; Workspace settings (in .vscode/settings.json) apply to the current project only.

q: What is the difference between User Settings and Workspace Settings?
a:
User Settings apply globally to every project you open.
Workspace Settings live in .vscode/settings.json inside the project and override User Settings.
Use Workspace Settings for project-specific formatting, linting, or extension configs.

q: How do you open the integrated terminal in VS Code?
a:
Ctrl+` (backtick). You can have multiple terminals open -- use the + icon or Ctrl+Shift+` to create new ones.
The terminal runs in your project directory by default.

q: How do you split the editor into side-by-side panes?
a:
Ctrl+\ splits the editor right.
You can also drag a tab to the side of the editor.
Useful for viewing a playbook and its variables file, or code and tests, at the same time.

q: How do you toggle the sidebar (Explorer panel) on and off?
a:
Ctrl+B. This gives you more editing space.
The sidebar contains the Explorer, Search, Source Control, Extensions, and other panels.

q: How do you search across all files in a project?
a:
Ctrl+Shift+F opens the Search panel.
You can filter by file type (e.g. *.yml) using the "files to include" field.
Supports regex with the .* button.

q: How do you find and replace text in the current file?
a:
Ctrl+H opens find and replace.
Use Ctrl+D to select the next occurrence of the current word one at a time.
Ctrl+Shift+L selects all occurrences at once for multi-cursor editing.

q: What does Ctrl+Shift+E do in VS Code?
a:
Opens the Explorer panel (file tree).
From here you can create, rename, delete, and move files.
Right-click for context menu options.

q: How do you move a line up or down in VS Code?
a:
Alt+Up/Down moves the current line (or selection) up or down.
No need to cut and paste.
Alt+Shift+Up/Down copies the line instead of moving it.

q: How do you comment out a line or selection in VS Code?
a:
Ctrl+/ toggles line comments.
Ctrl+Shift+A toggles block comments.
Works in any language -- VS Code uses the correct comment syntax for the file type.

q: How do you go to a specific line number in VS Code?
a:
Ctrl+G, then type the line number.
Or use Ctrl+P and type :42 to go to line 42 of the current file.

q: How do you install an extension in VS Code?
a:
Ctrl+Shift+X opens the Extensions panel.
Search for the extension name and click Install.
You can also install from the command line: code --install-extension publisher.extension-name

q: How do you zoom in and out in VS Code?
a:
Ctrl+= to zoom in, Ctrl+- to zoom out, Ctrl+0 to reset.
This scales the entire UI.
To change just the editor font size, modify "editor.fontSize" in settings.

q: How do you select multiple lines or make multiple cursors?
a:
Alt+Click places additional cursors.
Ctrl+Alt+Up/Down adds cursors on adjacent lines.
Ctrl+D selects the next occurrence of the current word and adds a cursor there.
Useful for editing multiple YAML keys or variable names at once.

q: What is the VS Code Activity Bar?
a:
The vertical icon strip on the far left side.
It switches between Explorer, Search, Source Control, Run/Debug, and Extensions panels.
You can right-click it to hide icons you do not use.

q: How do you close all open editor tabs at once?
a:
Ctrl+K Ctrl+W closes all tabs.
Ctrl+W closes just the active tab.
You can also right-click a tab for options like "Close Others" or "Close to the Right".

q: What is the minimap in VS Code and how do you toggle it?
a:
The minimap is the small code preview on the right side of the editor.
Toggle it with View > Minimap, or set "editor.minimap.enabled": false in settings.

q: How do you use breadcrumbs in VS Code?
a:
Breadcrumbs show the file path and code structure at the top of the editor (e.g. src > main.py > class Foo > method bar).
Click any segment to navigate.
Toggle with View > Breadcrumbs.

q: How do you fold (collapse) and unfold code blocks?
a:
Ctrl+Shift+[ folds the current block.
Ctrl+Shift+] unfolds it.
Ctrl+K Ctrl+0 folds everything.
Ctrl+K Ctrl+J unfolds everything.
Useful for navigating large YAML files or playbooks.

q: How do you peek at a definition without leaving your current file?
a:
Alt+F12 opens a peek window showing the definition inline.
F12 (Go to Definition) navigates to the definition file.
Shift+F12 shows all references to that symbol.

q: What does the bottom status bar in VS Code show you?
a:
The blue/purple bar at the bottom shows: current branch (Git), errors/warnings count, line and column number, file encoding, line ending type (LF/CRLF), language mode, and indentation (spaces/tabs).
Click any item to change it.

q: How do you change the file language mode in VS Code?
a:
Click the language name in the bottom status bar (e.g. "Plain Text") and select the correct language.
This enables proper syntax highlighting.
You can also use Ctrl+K M.
Useful when VS Code does not detect YAML or Jinja2 files correctly.

q: How do you format a document in VS Code?
a:
Shift+Alt+F formats the entire file using the configured formatter.
You can also enable "editor.formatOnSave": true in settings to format automatically when you save.

q: What is a VS Code Workspace file (.code-workspace)?
a:
A JSON file that defines a multi-root workspace -- multiple folders opened together with shared settings.
Created via File > Save Workspace As.
Useful when your project spans multiple repos (e.g. app + infra + config).

q: How do you compare two files side by side in VS Code?
a:
Select the first file in Explorer, then Ctrl+click the second file.
Right-click and choose "Compare Selected".
Or from the Command Palette: "File: Compare Active File With..."

q: How do you use the built-in Git support in VS Code?
a:
Ctrl+Shift+G opens the Source Control panel.
It shows changed files, lets you stage/unstage with +/- buttons, write commit messages, and push/pull.
The gutter also shows inline change indicators.

q: How do you view a file diff in VS Code?
a:
In the Source Control panel (Ctrl+Shift+G), click any changed file to see a side-by-side diff.
Deletions show in red, additions in green.
You can also click the gutter change indicators in the editor.

q: What does the GitLens extension add to VS Code?
a:
GitLens adds inline blame annotations (who changed each line and when), rich commit history browsing, file and line history views, and visual branch comparisons.
Essential for understanding unfamiliar codebases.

q: How do you resolve merge conflicts in VS Code?
a:
VS Code highlights conflict markers and shows clickable options above each conflict: Accept Current, Accept Incoming, Accept Both, or Compare Changes.
After resolving all conflicts, stage the file and commit.

q: What extension should you install for Python development in VS Code?
a:
The Microsoft Python extension (ms-python.python).
It provides IntelliSense, linting, debugging, Jupyter notebook support, and automatic virtual environment detection.

q: How do you select a Python interpreter in VS Code?
a:
Ctrl+Shift+P then type "Python: Select Interpreter".
Choose the correct virtual environment or system Python.
The selected interpreter appears in the status bar.
This determines which packages are available for autocomplete and linting.

q: How do you run a Python file in VS Code?
a:
Click the play button (top right) or use Ctrl+Shift+P > "Python: Run Python File in Terminal".
You can also right-click in the editor and select "Run Python File in Terminal".
The output appears in the integrated terminal.

q: How do you debug a Python script in VS Code?
a:
Set breakpoints by clicking the gutter (red dot appears).
Press F5 to start debugging.
VS Code pauses at breakpoints and shows variables, call stack, and watch expressions.
For the first run, it creates a launch.json config.

q: How do you run Python tests in VS Code?
a:
Ctrl+Shift+P > "Python: Configure Tests". Select pytest or unittest and the test directory.
The Testing panel (flask icon in Activity Bar) shows all discovered tests with pass/fail status and lets you run or debug individual tests.

q: What is Pylance and why should you use it with VS Code?
a:
Pylance is Microsoft's fast Python language server.
It provides better autocomplete, type checking, auto-imports, and semantic highlighting than the default.
Install it alongside the Python extension for the best experience.

q: How do you configure Python linting in VS Code?
a:
Install ruff or flake8, then install the Ruff extension (charliermarsh.ruff) which provides linting and formatting.
Errors appear as squiggly underlines in the editor and in the Problems panel.

q: What extension should you install for Ansible development in VS Code?
a:
The Red Hat Ansible extension (redhat.ansible).
It provides YAML syntax highlighting for playbooks, module autocomplete, inline documentation, and integration with ansible-lint for real-time error checking.

q: How do you get Ansible module autocomplete working in VS Code?
a:
Install the Red Hat Ansible extension and make sure ansible is installed in your Python environment.
The extension uses ansible-doc to provide autocomplete for module names and parameters.
Set "ansible.python.interpreterPath" if needed.

q: How do you associate YAML files with Ansible in VS Code?
How do you run an Ansible playbook from VS Code?
a:
Open the integrated terminal (Ctrl+`) and run ansible-playbook directly.
Or create a task in .vscode/tasks.json with the ansible-playbook command, then run it via Ctrl+Shift+P > "Tasks: Run Task".

q: How do you enable ansible-lint in VS Code?
a:
Install ansible-lint (pip install ansible-lint) and the Red Hat Ansible extension.
The extension runs ansible-lint automatically and shows warnings inline.
Configure rules in .ansible-lint at the project root.

q: How do you navigate between Ansible roles and included files in VS Code?
a:
Ctrl+Click on a role name, include path, or import_tasks path to jump to that file.
The Ansible extension supports Go to Definition (F12) for role references and variable files.
Use Ctrl+P to quickly open files by name.

q: What VS Code settings help when editing Ansible YAML files?
a:
Key settings for .vscode/settings.json:
"editor.tabSize": 2 (Ansible standard)
"editor.insertSpaces": true
"editor.autoIndent": "full"
"files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true
These prevent common YAML indentation errors.

q: What extension provides Docker support in VS Code?
a:
The Microsoft Docker extension (ms-azuretools.vscode-docker).
It adds Dockerfile and docker-compose.yml syntax highlighting, image/container management in the sidebar, and the ability to build, run, and attach to containers.

q: How do you view running Docker containers in VS Code?
a:
The Docker extension adds a Docker icon to the Activity Bar.
Click it to see running containers, images, registries, and networks.
Right-click a container to view logs, open a shell, stop, or remove it.

q: How do you attach VS Code to a running Docker container?
a:
Right-click the container in the Docker panel and select "Attach Visual Studio Code".
This opens a new VS Code window connected inside the container, so you can edit files and run commands as if you were inside it.

q: What extension provides Kubernetes support in VS Code?
a:
The Kubernetes extension (ms-kubernetes-tools.vscode-kubernetes-tools).
It shows clusters, namespaces, pods, services, and other resources in the sidebar.
You can view logs, describe resources, and apply manifests directly from VS Code.

q: How do you apply a Kubernetes manifest from VS Code?
a:
Right-click the YAML file in the Explorer and select "Apply" (requires the Kubernetes extension).
Or use the terminal: kubectl apply -f manifest.yaml.
The YAML extension with Kubernetes schema validation will catch errors before you apply.

q: How do you get YAML schema validation for Kubernetes manifests in VS Code?
How do you set up VS Code for Terraform development?
a:
Install the HashiCorp Terraform extension.
It provides syntax highlighting, autocomplete for resources and data sources, format-on-save, and Go to Definition for module references.
Enable: "editor.formatOnSave": true

q: How does VS Code help with Terraform variable references?
a:
The Terraform extension supports Go to Definition (F12) and hover documentation for variables, resources, and module references.
Ctrl+Click a var.name reference to jump to its declaration in variables.tf.

q: How do you connect to a remote server via SSH in VS Code?
a:
Install the Remote-SSH extension.
Ctrl+Shift+P > "Remote-SSH: Connect to Host" > enter user@hostname.
VS Code opens a new window connected to the remote server.
You edit files remotely but the UI runs locally.

q: How do you configure SSH hosts for quick access in VS Code?
a:
Edit your ~/.ssh/config file with Host entries:
Host myserver
  HostName 10.0.1.5
  User admin
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa
These appear in the Remote-SSH host list for one-click connections.

q: How do you forward a port from a remote server in VS Code?
a:
When connected via Remote-SSH, open the Ports panel (Ctrl+Shift+P > "Forward a Port").
Enter the remote port number.
VS Code maps it to localhost so you can access remote web servers or APIs from your local browser.

q: How do you enable better YAML editing in VS Code?
a:
Install the Red Hat YAML extension. It provides:
- Schema validation (Kubernetes, Docker Compose, GitHub Actions, etc.)
- Autocomplete based on schemas
- Hover documentation
- Proper error highlighting for indentation issues

q: How do you auto-format JSON files in VS Code?
a:
Open the JSON file and press Shift+Alt+F to format.
VS Code has built-in JSON formatting.
For YAML, you need the Red Hat YAML extension.
Enable "editor.formatOnSave": true to auto-format every time you save.

q: How do you quickly duplicate a line in VS Code?
a:
Shift+Alt+Down copies the current line below.
Shift+Alt+Up copies it above.
No need to select, copy, and paste. Works with selections too.

q: How do you delete an entire line in VS Code?
a:
Ctrl+Shift+K deletes the current line instantly.
No need to select the line first.

q: How do you indent or outdent selected lines in VS Code?
a:
Tab indents the selected lines.
Shift+Tab outdents them.
This works on multi-line selections, which is very useful for fixing YAML indentation.

q: How do you open a file in VS Code from the terminal?
a:
Type: code filename.yml
This works from the integrated terminal or any system terminal where VS Code is in your PATH.
Use code -r filename.yml to reuse the current window.

q: What is Zen Mode in VS Code?
a:
Ctrl+K Z enters Zen Mode -- a distraction-free fullscreen editing view that hides the sidebar, status bar, and tabs.
Press Escape twice to exit.
Useful for focused editing of long playbooks or scripts.

q: How do you open a recent project or file in VS Code?
a:
Ctrl+R shows a list of recent folders and workspaces.
Ctrl+P shows recent files in the current project.
These are faster than navigating the file system every time.

q: How do you change the color theme in VS Code?
a:
Ctrl+K Ctrl+T opens the theme picker.
Popular dark themes: One Dark Pro, Dracula, GitHub Dark.
You can preview each theme by arrowing through the list before selecting.

q: What does the Problems panel show in VS Code?
a:
Ctrl+Shift+M opens the Problems panel.
It lists all errors and warnings from linters, language servers, and extensions across all open files.
Click any item to jump to that line.
The count also shows in the status bar.

q: How do you use snippets in VS Code?
a:
Type a snippet prefix and press Tab to expand.
For example, in Python files type "def" and Tab to get a function template.
Ctrl+Shift+P > "Snippets: Configure User Snippets" to create your own custom snippets.

q: How do you set per-language settings in VS Code?
